hypotheses.statement: Daily ACV consumption (5, 10 or 15 mL) for 4-12 weeks reduces anthropometric variables (weight, BMI, waist/hip circumference, body fat ratio) relative to baseline and to placebo.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Our findings showed that daily consumption of the three doses of ACV for a duration of between 4 and 12 weeks is associated with significant reductions in anthropometric variables (weight, body mass index, waist/hip circumferences and body fat ratio), blood glucose, triglyceride and cholesterol levels.

hypotheses.provenance_quote: The consumption of ACV also led to a time and dose dependent decrease in serum glucose, serum triglyceride and serum cholesterol levels.

hypotheses.statement: Effects are dose-dependent, with 15 mL most effective.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: A dose of 15 mL of ACV for a duration of 12 weeks seems to be the most effective dose in reducing these three blood biochemical parameters.

findings.location: Table 2, Weight row, Group 3 week 12 vs Group 4 (placebo) week 12
findings.quote: Group 3 ... 70.2±25.0*†‡ | Group 4 (placebo) ... 78.8±28.6†‡ ; †p<0.05; compared with group 1 within a specific week. ‡p<0.05; compared with group 2 within a specific week.
findings.notes: The paper's headline claim -- the highest ACV dose beats placebo on weight at week 12 -- is not recoverable from the paper's own descriptive statistics. Across the entire rounding interval implied by the printed precision, the achievable p lies in [0.214, 0.226]; p<0.05 is unreachable by any rounding of the reported means and SDs. Monte Carlo hit rate for the reported p is exactly 0. The paper states the only test used was an independent t-test ('Significant differences between groups were determined by using an independent t-test'), so this is the test the tool reproduces. The driver is the enormous reported weight SDs (25-28.6 kg), which are themselves anomalous (see weight_sd_incoherent_with_bmi_sd).

findings.location: Table 2, Weight row, Group 2 week 12 vs Group 1 week 12
findings.quote: Group 1 ... 73.9±23.7*‡ | Group 2 ... 71.9±26.1*† ; †p<0.05; compared with group 1 within a specific week.
findings.notes: Group 2 at week 12 carries a dagger marking it significantly different from group 1, but the two groups' reported means differ by 2.0 kg against SDs of 23.7-26.1 kg: recalculated p = 0.76, fifteen times the claimed threshold. This is a second, independent instance of the same pattern as weight_w12_g3_vs_placebo_not_significant.

findings.location: Table 2, Weight row, Group 3 week 12 vs Group 1 week 0 baseline comparison (dose-dependence claim)
findings.notes: The paper's largest single weight change (group 3, week 0 to week 12, a 7.0 kg drop) is marked significant, but recalculates to p = 0.30 as an independent t-test -- the test the paper says it used. NOTE the design caveat: week 0 vs week 12 in the SAME participants is a PAIRED comparison, and an independent t-test is the wrong test for it (see design_paired_data_analysed_as_independent). Under a paired test with a high pre/post correlation this change could well be significant; that is why this finding is 'suspicious' rather than 'highly_suspicious'. The between-group findings above do not have that escape route.

inputs.comparisons_made: within-subject week 0 vs weeks 4, 8, 12 in the same 30 participants per arm; plus 4 arms x 3 timepoints x 7 variables of between-group contrasts

computed.design_mismatch: repeated-measures (groups x time) design analysed with independent-samples t-tests
computed.multiplicity: ~100+ pairwise contrasts marked in Tables 2-3 with no stated correction

findings.reproduction: Not a numeric check -- no CLI form. Design assessment recorded per rulebook rule 5 from the quoted Methods sentence and table footnotes.
findings.notes: Two distinct methodological problems, recorded together because they share one source sentence. (1) The paper reports only one test -- the independent t-test -- yet the asterisked comparisons are week-0-versus-later-week within the SAME participants, which are paired. Treating correlated observations as independent is a design error in either direction: it inflates the SE for the within-subject contrasts (making the recalculated p's above conservative) while no repeated-measures or mixed model is reported anywhere. (2) Tables 2 and 3 mark well over 100 pairwise contrasts (4 arms x 3 post-baseline timepoints x 7 outcomes, plus between-arm daggers) with no multiplicity correction stated. No assumption checks (normality, homogeneity of variance) are reported.

findings.location: Table 1, Weight (kg) and BMI (kg/m2) rows, all four groups
findings.notes: The three anthropometric SDs cannot describe one set of 30 people. BMI is DERIVED from weight and height, and the paper's own stated inclusion criterion confines BMI to 27-34 kg/m2 -- a stated constraint, not an assumed one. The reported BMI SD of ~3.0 uses 87% of the maximum possible spread for that 7-point window, so BMI is near-maximally dispersed within its bound. Yet weight carries an SD of 27-28.6 kg and height an SD of 20-22 cm, each ~79-89% of its own plausibility ceiling. A cohort whose weight ranges over roughly 50-110 kg and whose height ranges over roughly 140-190 cm while every member stays inside BMI 27-34 is not constructible in any ordinary way: the height SD of 20 cm alone is far outside population norms for any age band (adult female SD ~6.5 cm), and 12-25 year-olds spanning that height range would not share a 7-point BMI window. These inflated SDs are also precisely what makes the between-group tests non-significant (see weight_w12_g3_vs_placebo_not_significant). Severity held at 'suspicious' per rulebook rule 4: the weight and height ceilings rest on ranges I supplied (50-110 kg, 140-190 cm), and are named here; only the BMI bound is stated by the paper.

findings.location: Table 2, Weight vs BMI rows, Group 3 week 12 vs Group 4 (placebo) week 12

computed.ratio: BMI p is ~3400x smaller than the weight p for the same contrast

findings.notes: This is the internal contradiction that makes the SD anomaly hard to explain innocently. BMI is computed FROM weight and height in the same 30 people, so the two rows describe one underlying fact. The BMI contrast is strongly significant (p = 6.4e-5) while the identical weight contrast is not remotely so (p = 0.22). For both to be true, the weight SD would have to be inflated roughly nine-fold relative to the BMI SD -- which is what Table 1 in fact reports. The BMI rows behave like real data from a BMI 27-34 cohort; the weight and height rows do not, yet all three are presented as measurements of the same participants.

findings.notes: Rulebook rule 11's inverse: identical records of the same facts SHOULD match, and here 8 of 12 do -- correctly, since both blocks describe the same 120 participants at week 0 (sample_id set so the matches are not false-flagged). The finding is the 4 that do NOT. The same baseline measurement is printed with two different values in two tables of one paper. The placebo FBS discrepancy matters most: Table 1 gives 113.6 mg/dL, which is 6.5 mg/dL below group 1 and would make the placebo arm significantly different from group 1 AT BASELINE (recalculated p = 0.036, an apparent randomisation failure), whereas Table 3's 118.6 mg/dL sits unremarkably among the other arms. The Table 1 group-3 FBS SD of 7.2 is likewise the single tightest SD in the table and becomes 12.2 in Table 3. Confirmed byte-identical in both the markdown extraction and the source PDF (pages 3 and 5), so this is not an extraction artefact.

findings.location: Table 1, FBS row, Group 4 (placebo) vs Group 1

reported.claim: no baseline difference is reported or discussed anywhere in the paper

findings.notes: Taking Table 1 at face value, the placebo arm's baseline fasting glucose differs significantly from group 1's (p = 0.036) -- a baseline imbalance in a randomised trial that the paper never mentions. Under Table 3's week-0 value (118.6) the imbalance disappears entirely. The two tables therefore imply opposite conclusions about whether randomisation succeeded on this variable, which is why the discrepancy in table1_vs_table3_baseline_contradiction is consequential rather than a typo of no effect.

With n=30 every percentage must be a multiple of 1/30 = 3.33%. 11/30 = 36.7% and 19/30 = 63.3%; the table prints 36.6 and 63.4. The counts (n=11, n=19) are printed alongside and are correct, and the four groups' counts sum correctly to the stated 46 men and 74 women, so this is almost certainly a rounding/transcription slip rather than fabricated data. Recorded as 'impossible' because that is the arithmetic verdict, but it is the weakest finding in this review and should not be presented as evidence of anything beyond sloppy proofreading. GRIM-consistent for all three other groups (40.0/60.0, 33.3/66.7, 43.3/56.7). NOTE: the reproduction command uses the CLI grim verb with proportion bounds; grim_percentage itself is MCP-only and has no CLI form.

Corroborates gender_pct_group3_grim from the other direction: no denominator at all between 5 and 40 can produce either 36.6% or 63.4%, so the pair cannot share any plausible sample size. Same caveat -- consistent with a rounding slip, not a data-integrity signal on its own.

n=30 is among the viable denominators for group 1's 40.0/60.0 split. Groups 2 (33.3/66.7) and 4 (43.3/56.7) are likewise exact multiples of 1/30. Only group 3 fails, which supports reading it as an isolated rounding error.

findings.location: Table 1, all 11 baseline rows across 4 groups
findings.quote: Table 1 Baseline demographic, anthropometric and biochemical variables of the three apple cider vinegar groups (group 1, 2 and 3) and the placebo group (group 4)

inputs.rows: Age, Weight, Height, BMI, Waist, Hip, BFR, FBS, TG, TC (continuous, 4 groups x n=30) + Gender (categorical 2x4)

findings.notes: Tested for the Carlisle/Fujii under-dispersion signature (rulebook rule 1: uniformly HIGH baseline p-values are the red flag, never reassurance). tau-hat = 1.44 does point mildly toward under-dispersion, and three rows are strikingly uniform across arms (Weight p = 0.991, Height p = 0.990, Age p = 0.931). But the result does NOT survive the correlation-aware null: the 90% CI [0.76, 16.15] straddles 1, the K-S test against U(0,1) is non-significant (p = 0.16), and the CSF cross-check gives similarity p = 0.19. Weight, height, BMI, waist, hip and BFR are mutually predictive, leaving only ~2 effectively independent rows, so this table is too small and too correlated to support a baseline-uniformity finding. Reported as consistent -- the anomalies in this paper lie elsewhere. An earlier exploratory csf_test run of mine used illustrative rather than reported p-values and was discarded; this row supersedes it.

findings.location: Discussion, 'reduced the body weight by 6-8 kg and BMIs by 2.7-3.0 points'; Table 2
findings.quote: daily oral intake of ACV for 12 weeks reduced the body weight by 6–8 kg and BMIs by 2.7–3.0 points.

reported.claimed_effect: 6-8 kg weight loss, 2.7-3.0 BMI points over 12 weeks

findings.notes: As a standardised effect the weight contrast is unremarkable (g = 0.32, at the medicine_rct median of 0.3) -- but only because the inflated SDs deflate it. In RAW clinical terms the claim is extreme: an unsupervised 15 mL/day vinegar dose with no dietary restriction producing 6-8 kg loss and a 2.7-3.0 point BMI drop in 12 weeks is comparable to or better than GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide ~6% body mass at 12 weeks), from an intervention with no plausible mechanism of that magnitude. I report the tool's verdict of 'consistent' faithfully; the raw-scale implausibility is a judgement for the editorial stage and is flagged here rather than scored, since the benchmark comparison is on the standardised scale.

findings.location: Table 1, BMI row; Methods inclusion criteria
findings.notes: The BMI SD does not violate the paper's own stated inclusion bound, so there is no impossibility here. It is however near-maximal (87% of the ceiling), which would require participants stacked at both ends of the 27-34 window rather than clustered mid-range. Recorded as consistent; its significance is as the companion to weight_sd_incoherent_with_bmi_sd, where the same 30 people carry a weight SD nine times larger.

findings.location: Table 1, BMI row, Group 1; Methods inclusion criteria

reported.required_proportion: 100% of participants must have BMI <= 34 by inclusion criterion

findings.notes: Under a normal model with the reported mean and SD, only 86% of group 1 would fall below the BMI 34 ceiling, yet the inclusion criterion requires 100%. The tool returns 'consistent' (binomial p = 0.028 is not decisive at n=30, and a truncated distribution is expected under an inclusion rule), so I record it as such. It is a mild corroboration that the reported SDs are wider than a genuinely BMI-27-34-truncated sample would show.

findings.notes: statcheck recovered zero NHST triples because the paper reports NO test statistics anywhere -- not one t, F, chi-squared, df or exact p appears in the text, tables or footnotes. Every claim rests on bare 'p<0.05' / 'p>0.05' markers. This is itself the reportable result: it removes the normal route to verification and is why the recalculations above had to be driven from the descriptive statistics instead. It also means STALT cannot be run (no recoverable exact p behind the thresholds where the recalculated value exceeds the threshold rather than falling below it).

findings.reproduction: Not a numeric check -- no CLI form. Recorded per rulebook rule 7 from the quoted statements.
findings.notes: Three reporting concerns recorded together under rulebook rule 7. (1) State-but-withhold: the availability statement promises supplementary data, but no supplement accompanies the paper and no participant-level data appear. (2) Diet diaries and physical activity were collected and are used to support the causal claim ('the diet diary and physical activity did not differ among the three treatment groups... suggesting that the decrease... was caused by ACV intake') yet no supporting numbers, tests or p-values for either are reported anywhere. (3) Zero attrition: 120 adolescents/young adults enrolled and 120 analysed at weeks 0, 4, 8 and 12 with no dropouts, no missing measurements and no adverse events over 12 weeks of daily unsupervised vinegar consumption -- implausibly complete for this population and duration. Also note no a-priori power analysis is stated, so verify_power_analysis could not be run.

unchecked.location: Tables 2 and 3 — the majority of the ~130 individually asterisked/daggered cell comparisons
unchecked.reason: Tables 2 and 3 mark well over 100 pairwise contrasts with bare p<0.05 symbols. I recalculated a targeted, pre-specified subset: the headline dose-vs-placebo weight contrast, its BMI counterpart, a second between-arm weight contrast, and the largest within-arm weight change. Exhaustive recalculation of every cell was not run; the four recalculated contrasts were chosen because they carry the abstract and conclusion claims, and three of the four failed. A full sweep would likely surface more of the same pattern but was not performed, so no claim is made about the unchecked cells.

unchecked.location: Waist, hip, BFR, TG and TC significance markers in Tables 2 and 3
unchecked.reason: Not individually recalculated. These outcomes have modest SDs relative to their means (unlike weight and height) and their within-arm changes are small, so the independent-vs-paired test question dominates their interpretation; without knowing the pre/post correlation the paper never reports, a recalculation would be uninformative rather than probative.

STALT requires a recoverable exact p that is far BELOW the stated threshold. Here the recalculated values run in the opposite direction (above the threshold), which is captured by the recalc/RIVETS findings instead. No test statistics, df or exact p-values are printed anywhere in the paper, so there is nothing further to recover.

unchecked.location: A-priori power analysis / sample size justification
unchecked.reason: None is stated. verify_power_analysis requires a stated effect size, alpha and target power to reproduce a calculation; with no power statement at all there is nothing to verify. Recorded as a reporting gap in data_availability_state_but_withhold rather than as a tool failure.

unchecked.location: Baseline eating-habit and lifestyle percentages (98.3% non-vegetarian, 89% high eating frequency, 87% no family history, 98% no childhood obesity, 6.7% therapeutic diet)
unchecked.reason: These are reported for the whole cohort in prose with no per-group breakdown and, critically, no explicit denominator — GRIM on a percentage requires a certain n. 98.3% and 6.7% are consistent with n=120 (118/120 = 98.3%, 8/120 = 6.7%), but 89%, 87% and 98% are printed to 0 decimals, which is too coarse to constrain a denominator of 120.
